Koniguldon had just finished assigning the next watch when Formis returned to their temporary mountain camp.

"It was a hag... a male. He didn't give his name. In exchange for a handful of choice metals and a few gemstones, he left a riddle."

The leader tried not to let his impatience show as he folded his mighty arms and listened.

"From waters deep, I came. In shallow waters I sleep. Always eating, never drinking, three tails... I am my own thief."

"Meaningless slag," Koniguldon rumbled. "If the hag returns, I'll speak with him myself. Go rest now."

Formis saluted, then wandered off.

The leader strolled through the makeshift camp, taking comfort in the sounds of heavy hammers and pickaxes rising and falling in the distance. If the mission was a success, his people would never hunger again. If. But Koniguldon was no star-crossed fool. He believed firmly in the maxim that if things seemed too good to be true, they probably were.

He found Jamus taking a night time bath in a small mountain stream. For a moment, he watched the perfectly formed being rub off the dirt and grime of the day's labors in the soft moonlight. When he realized he was being watched, Jamus moved to cover himself with a nearby boulder.

"Sir," he said awkwardly.

Koniguldon came close. "Do you think the watches I've set are sufficient? Will we have ample time in case we are attacked?"

Jamus thought for a few seconds before replying. "Yes. But... what enemy could pose any threat to us? We are so much stronger than the mere flesh creatures we have encountered."

The leader sat on a rocky outcropping and rested his chin on his fist. He made a grumbling sound as he considered that. "Aye. So far, we have proven the stronger. If slower."

"It hardly seems to make a difference," Jamus said. "If no arrow can penetrate us, nor any sword crack our skins."

Koniguldon grinned at him without pleasure. "There may be more things beneath the black sky of this world than are dreamt of in that rocky head of yours." Gently, he touched his friend's hand. "I'm glad you agreed to join the expedition. You've been like an extra right hand; a real asset. Your father..."

"I don't care what my father says," Jamus said with sudden anger. "I'm proud I came. He would have us dwelling in the same old moldy rat caves until the end of time."

Koniguldon grunted with understanding, as he subtly admired the well-formed curve of his underling's waist. "Try not to judge him too harshly. He wants the best for you."

There came a sound then. It was very weak, and far off.

"Did you hear that?" Jamus asked.

"No," Koniguldon replied. But he had heard something. A strange rustling... or was it a stifled whimper? He wasn't absolutely certain he'd really heard anything at all. "Go to camp. Take some rest. We'll talk at length in the morning."

Jamus smiled. "All right. And thank you for what you said about my father. Maybe I am being harsh." He stepped from behind the boulder, unashamed, looking up into his master's eyes. Then he headed back into camp.

Koniguldon sighed, and splashed himself with cold water. The burdens of command were many.

Something about sitting here alone becoming increasingly wet and satisfied made him feel drowsy. There was something misleading about this place... this entire mountain. He needed time to think things over by himself. The others were useful, but they distracted him. Sometimes he wished he were deaf so he could hear neither their labors nor their complaints.

There came that sound again. Closer, but still too quiet and unimportant to alarm him. Sitting lazilly in the stream, he allowed his heavy metallic eyelids to close.

When he next opened them, they were crawling on him, struggling to penetrate his thick skin with their hoofs, horns and mandibles.

He tried to stand, but there were hundreds of them: thin, hard black legs, powerful pincher jaws, horns, and filthy white fur. Even with his immense strength he was barely able to rise. One of his mighty hands closed around the throat of one of the monsters. As two more of them fell from on top of him, he finally saw what he was holding.

It was a large goat... or something similar. But it had, in addition to horns, long black antennae, and huge gnashing jaws like a soldier ant.

It had four crooked nimble legs like a goat... but also six long, squirming legs, like those of an ant.

It had black armor plates covering its body, but also dirty white fur. Koniguldon laughed.

Then he saw more of them swarming over the ledge toward him, and he stopped laughing.

Occasionally eps, pdf, or something else, but it's been my experience that tiff is the default. I can almost guarantee it's because the people you are working with are running old software or are working with others who are working with old software. TIFF is lossless, but is for raster graphics (graphics made up with little dots). A lot of publications work in vector graphics applications (such as the push over from a direct Photoshop design structure into a Publisher/Adobe AI setup). Once people realized that there were formats that could transcend software limitations, OS requirements, etc. they began jumping onto it.

Could it also be because of how the original images (raw data) are created? Let's say you take an image with a microscope - naturally it's going to be a raster image because of the way the image is physically created. I'm not sure how the conversion between raster and vector is done, but I imagine it would take quite a bit of manipulation. Generally speaking, data like that is supposed to be presented with minimal processing. Maybe it's just easier to have one standard for all types of images than to have different standards for each type of image?

In short, yes. That's one reason.

In long: Well, you can't really take a photo (raster by nature, pixels of color) and convert it to vector (shapes drawn with math) without effectively turning it into something it's not (and also not preserving integrity of the image, after all... If it can be converted to a vector, it could have been created as a vector to begin with) in that manner; however, there are softwares out there for printing that require certain formats which by their very nature can mimic the support of both formats. PDF (portable document format) eliminates their need to convert anything. It permits them to say "send this one format that anyone can create with their source material (and for free)."

The reason for mentioning the vector graphics applications (like AI) is that people began utilizing only those applications to handle their publication graphics... And typically people don't want to learn how to import/convert anything. So they'd use Illustrator for their own in-house graphics (or perhaps it's something that someone else chose and they came into using it and don't want to learn something else because it'd damage production speeds) and want it in one format or another because they're comfortable. Remember, Adobe's software is/was industry standard for graphics manipulation for many years. It's only now that people are exploring FOSS software that they are breaking free of the generalization of the graphics industry.
